Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The Court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint without converting this motion into one for summary judgment.**

Rule 12(d) requires conversion to summary judgment when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). The Ninth Circuit has long held that this rule is not triggered when a court considers documents that the complaint incorporates by reference. Those documents are treated as part of the complaint, so they are not "outside the pleadings."

**A. The incorporation-by-reference doctrine is settled in this Circuit.**

A court "may consider evidence on which the complaint necessarily relies if: (1) the complaint refers to the document; (2) the document is central to the plaintiff's claim; and (3) no party questions the authenticity of the copy attached to the 12(b)(6) motion." *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006). A court may do so "without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003). The rule reaches further than documents the complaint expressly quotes or attaches. It applies where "the plaintiff's claim depends on the contents of a document, the defendant attaches the document to its motion to dismiss, and the parties do not dispute the authenticity of the document, even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege the contents of that document in the complaint." *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). The Ninth Circuit adopted this rule in *Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002). It has applied the rule consistently since. *See Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010); *Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A.*, 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012).

**B. The doctrine prevents plaintiffs from avoiding dismissal by selective pleading.**

The Ninth Circuit has explained that the doctrine "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). Without the doctrine, a plaintiff could defeat a Rule 12(b)(6) motion by characterizing a document in the complaint in a way its text does not support. The doctrine also serves efficiency. When a plaintiff's claim rests on a document, the Court should not have to ignore that document and wait for summary judgment to read it. *See Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. Once a document is incorporated, the Court may treat it "as part of the complaint, and thus . . . assume that its contents are true for purposes of a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6)." *Id.*

**C. The doctrine has limits, and each is satisfied here.**

*Khoja* cautions that the doctrine is not a way to introduce disputed facts at the pleading stage. A court may not use an incorporated document to resolve factual disputes against the plaintiff. *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. Nor may it take notice of the truth of disputed facts in a document. *Lee v. City of Los Angeles*, 250 F.3d 668, 689 (9th Cir. 2001). Defendant's motion respects those limits. Defendant relies on the documents for what they say, not to contradict well-pleaded facts.

Each requirement is met here. [Insert record cites.] First, the Complaint refers to [DOCUMENT] at paragraphs [__]. Second, the document is central to Plaintiff's claim. The claim for [__] depends on the terms of [DOCUMENT], and Plaintiff cannot state that claim without relying on it. *See Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076. Third, Plaintiff has not questioned the authenticity of the copy attached as Exhibit [__] to the [Declaration of ___]. *See Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448.

Because the Complaint incorporates [DOCUMENT] by reference, the Court may consider it in full. That includes the provisions the Complaint omits, such as [describe]. Considering the document does not convert the motion under Rule 12(d). *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908; *Davis*, 691 F.3d at 1160.

**D. Conclusion**

The Court should consider Exhibit [__] in resolving Defendant's Rule 12(b)(6) motion and should decline to convert the motion into one for summary judgment.
